nameStory: White ash gets its name from the pale, whitish underside of its leaves that flash silver when the wind blows through the canopy. The wood is also notably lighter in color than other ash species, with a creamy white sapwood that made it highly prized by early settlers and continues to make it valuable for baseball bats and tool handles.
description: White ash is a tall, stately tree that can reach 80 feet high with a straight trunk and oval-shaped crown. It's a fast-growing native that was once a dominant forest tree throughout New England, valued for its strong, flexible wood. The tree has compound leaves made up of 5-9 leaflets arranged along a central stem, and produces distinctive winged seeds that helicopter down in fall. Unfortunately, many of New England's oldest white ashes have been killed by the invasive emerald ash borer, so most surviving trees today are younger and smaller.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 oval leaflets arranged opposite each other along a central stem, with one leaflet at the tip. The leaflets are smooth-edged or have tiny teeth, dark green above and distinctly whitish or pale green underneath.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Paddle-shaped winged seeds called samaras that hang in clusters and spin like helicopter blades when they fall. Each seed is about 1-2 inches long with the wing extending from one end only.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray bark with distinctive diamond-shaped furrows and interlacing ridges that create a crosshatch pattern on mature trees. Young trees have smoother, lighter gray bark.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall tree with a straight trunk and branches that grow opposite each other rather than alternating. The crown is oval-shaped and the tree often grows in mixed hardwood forests.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Dark brown to nearly black buds that sit opposite each other on the twigs. The buds are dome-shaped and feel smooth to the touch, making winter identification possible.

habitat: White ash thrives in rich, moist, well-drained soils throughout New England's mixed hardwood forests. You'll often find it growing alongside maples, oaks, hickories, and other hardwoods on slopes and in valleys up to about 2,000 feet elevation. It prefers slightly alkaline soils and is commonly found in areas with good soil depth and fertility.

seasonality.spring: Inconspicuous flowers appear before the leaves emerge, followed by the unfurling of compound leaves that start out bronze-green and mature to dark green.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy displays the characteristic pale undersides of leaves when wind moves through the tree. Seeds begin developing in hanging clusters.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant yellow to purple before dropping, and the distinctive winged seeds mature and begin falling, spinning as they descend.
seasonality.winter: Bare tree shows the diamond-patterned bark and distinctive dark buds arranged opposite each other on gray twigs.

funFact: White ash wood is so perfectly suited for baseball bats that major league players can often identify the specific ash tree their bat came from - the wood needs to have exactly the right combination of strength and flexibility, which only comes from trees grown in specific soil and climate conditions.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other compound-leaved trees like hickories and walnuts, but white ash is the only one with leaves arranged opposite each other on the branch - hickories and walnuts have alternating leaves. Memory trick: 'Ash is opposite, others alternate.'
contextualKnowledge: The emerald ash borer invasion has dramatically changed New England's forests since the 1990s, killing hundreds of millions of ash trees. Many communities have had to remove large numbers of dead ash trees, fundamentally altering the forest canopy and urban tree cover throughout the region.
compareHints: White ash differs from black ash by preferring drier, upland sites (black ash loves wet areas) and having leaflets with short stalks, while black ash leaflets attach directly to the main stem. Green ash has similar habitat preferences but typically has fewer leaflets per leaf (5-7 versus 7-9) and lacks the distinctly pale leaf undersides that give white ash its name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black ash differs from white ash by its preference for wet habitats, darker bark, and leaflets that lack individual stalks (sessile).
Green ash differs from white ash by its fuzzy, green-tinged leaf undersides (white ash has smooth, whitish undersides) and its greater tolerance for wet soils.
European ash differs from our native ashes primarily in its black, velvety winter buds - white ash has brown buds, green ash has smaller brown buds, and black ash has dark but pointed buds.
